candidates.label: A
candidates.abstract: A matrix engine can keep its arithmetic units busy without making proportional progress on useful computation. General matrix multiplications in DNN training expose this distinction through uneven matrix dimensions and unstructured zeros: a fixed systolic shape can leave multipliers idle while executing products that contribute nothing. SIGMA addresses both sources of inefficiency by allowing useful dot products to share a flexible compute fabric. Flex-DPEs group a logical row of multipliers, a Benes distribution network multicasts operands, and the Forwarding Adder Network routes partial sums for independently sized reductions. A bitmap identifies zero positions and guides useful operand placement; multiple Flex-DPEs compose into a Flex-DPU. Cycle-based analytical evaluation uses training-derived GEMMs and 16,384-PE accelerators, reporting the better of weight-stationary and input-stationary mappings. The study reports 5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs on sparse irregular workloads and approximately 3× over the compared sparse accelerators extended to GEMMs. These are kernel comparisons, not full training results. Flexibility increases compute-array area by 37.7%: a 28 nm implementation occupies 65.10 mm² and consumes 22.33 W at 500 MHz, excluding large SRAMs. Two GEMMs favor Eyeriss v2 because local retention avoids SIGMA's repeated operand streaming. Thus, flexible arithmetic placement improves useful execution, while operand locality, streaming sparsity, and bandwidth remain consequential limits.
introduction: General matrix multiplication provides a demanding target for DNN training accelerators because its dimensions and useful arithmetic need not match a fixed physical array. Uneven dimensions can strand multipliers at mapping boundaries, while unstructured zeros can occupy execution slots without contributing to the result. Improving stationary utilization therefore addresses only part of overall efficiency: the machine must also place useful operands and combine their products without imposing a single dot-product shape. Flexible dataflow mapping and compressed sparse execution are established architectural directions, represented by MAERI [kwon2018maeri] and SCNN [parashar2017scnn]. The question addressed here is how to bring flexible distribution and reduction together for irregular, sparse GEMMs.

SIGMA organizes a logical row of multipliers into Flexible Dot Product Engines, or Flex-DPEs, and composes these engines into a Flex-DPU for a GEMM. A Benes distribution fabric supports operand multicast, while the Forwarding Adder Network (FAN) routes partial sums so that independently sized dot products can share the reduction fabric. This separation gives operand placement and result accumulation the flexibility needed to accommodate different dot-product sizes. A bitmap identifies zero positions and guides placement of useful operands. Weight-stationary and input-stationary mappings provide alternative ways to retain operands; the evaluation reports the better mapping for each comparison. The mechanism consequently addresses both unused multiplier capacity and zero operations, rather than relying on a fixed array shape to suit every matrix.

We evaluate GEMMs with dimensions and sparsities drawn from GNMT, Transformer, NCF, and DeepBench using a cycle-based analytical model, a SCALE-sim systolic baseline, and accelerators scaled to 16,384 PEs. Sparse baselines include EIE, SCNN, OuterSPACE, Eyeriss v2, Packed Systolic, and Cambricon-X, extended to GEMMs with alternative orientations and sparsity placements explored. The study reports 5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs on sparse irregular workloads and approximately 3× over the compared sparse accelerators. Post-layout compute-array results at 28 nm and 500 MHz, using BF16 multiplication and FP32 addition, are 65.10 mm² and 22.33 W for SIGMA versus 47.27 mm² and 12.25 W for the systolic array; large SRAMs are excluded. The 37.7% area increase purchases flexibility, but does not eliminate data-supply costs: Eyeriss v2 wins on two GEMMs by retaining both operands locally while SIGMA streams one repeatedly. These results establish a GEMM-level tradeoff among flexible execution, locality, and bandwidth, without claiming full-training speedups.

candidates.abstract: General matrix multiplication in DNN training must accommodate uneven dimensions and unstructured zeros. A fixed systolic shape can therefore leave multipliers unused while still executing zero operations. We present SIGMA, which makes operand distribution and partial-sum reduction flexible enough for independently sized dot products to share an array. A bitmap guides placement of useful operands; a Benes multicast fabric feeds Flexible Dot Product Engines (Flex-DPEs), and the Forwarding Adder Network (FAN) routes their partial sums. Multiple Flex-DPEs form a Flex-DPU for each GEMM. A cycle-based analytical evaluation uses dimensions and sparsities from GNMT, Transformer, NCF, and DeepBench, with all modeled accelerators scaled to 16,384 PEs and the better of weight-stationary and input-stationary mappings reported for SIGMA. On sparse irregular workloads, the study reports 5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs and approximately 3× over compared sparse accelerators adapted to GEMMs. These are modeled GEMM results, not full training runs. In a 28 nm post-layout comparison at 500 MHz with BF16 multiplication and FP32 addition, flexibility raises compute-array area by 37.7%. SIGMA occupies 65.10 mm² and consumes 22.33 W, excluding large SRAMs. Bandwidth and repeated operand streaming remain limiting factors; Eyeriss v2 is faster on two evaluated GEMMs.
introduction: General matrix multiplication is a central computation in the DNN training workloads considered here, but its dimensions and useful work do not always match a fixed compute array. Uneven matrix dimensions can leave part of a systolic array idle, while unstructured zeros can consume operations without contributing to the result. Keeping an operand stationary does not by itself resolve either mismatch: the machine must place useful products on available multipliers and combine them into dot products of the required sizes. The design problem therefore extends beyond stationary utilization. Overall efficiency also depends on whether distribution and reduction can accommodate irregular work without stranding arithmetic resources.

Reconfigurable dataflow and sparse computation provide relevant starting points. MAERI addresses flexible dataflow mapping through reconfigurable interconnects [kwon2018maeri], while SCNN targets compressed-sparse convolutional networks [parashar2017scnn]. For training GEMMs, SIGMA couples flexible allocation of useful multiplications with flexible formation of their sums. It groups a logical row of multipliers into Flexible Dot Product Engines, or Flex-DPEs. A bitmap identifies zero positions and guides useful-operand placement; a Benes distribution fabric multicasts operands to the multipliers that need them. The Forwarding Adder Network (FAN) routes partial sums so that independently sized dot products can share the reduction fabric. Multiple Flex-DPEs compose into a Flex-DPU for a GEMM. Together, these choices let operand placement and reduction follow the available useful work instead of requiring every dot product to occupy the same fixed shape.

We evaluate SIGMA with a cycle-based analytical model and a SCALE-sim systolic baseline, scaling each modeled accelerator to 16,384 PEs. The GEMMs use dimensions and sparsities from GNMT, Transformer, NCF, and DeepBench; SIGMA reports the better of weight-stationary and input-stationary mappings. Comparisons extend EIE, SCNN, OuterSPACE, Eyeriss v2, Packed Systolic, and Cambricon-X to GEMMs and explore alternative matrix orientations and sparsity placements. The study reports 5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs on sparse irregular workloads and approximately 3× over the compared sparse accelerators. These results concern GEMMs rather than complete training execution. Flexibility also has a physical cost: post-layout compute arrays in commercial 28 nm technology at 500 MHz, using BF16 multiplication and FP32 addition, occupy 65.10 mm² and consume 22.33 W for SIGMA, versus 47.27 mm² and 12.25 W for the systolic array. The 37.7% area increase excludes large SRAMs, as do both power figures. Operand supply remains a constraint: Eyeriss v2 is faster on two GEMMs because it retains both operands locally while SIGMA streams one repeatedly. Streaming sparsity and bandwidth thus delimit the benefit of flexible compute allocation.
